sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

The lands around it are old and quarrelsome. Minor noble houses hold the river-farms, trade in favours, and pay well for stories that make their lineages look older than they are.

A few weeks ago she slipped away from his caravan at a river crossing in the night. She also carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, the gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers, with a curl of old parchment inside that may be a true blessing or just another forgery.

A weathered driver lounges on the box, picking his teeth. Before him a young page in a minor noble's livery, pale and sweating, is pressing a sealed letter into his hand and glancing over his shoulder. The wax seal is one you've seen in the ledger. On the tailboard behind them sits a locked, iron-bound strongbox, begging to be poked at.

I take the other path straight across the green at a brisk walk, cutting the brown-coated man off in the open before he reaches the gate, and call out warmly, "Friend! Forgive me, you look like a man who knows the way to the manor kitchens, I'm told there's supper there for pilgrims."

input.add_to_description: Gave his name as Garrow, a "hedge-carpenter looking for work", when Wren (Deception 20) walked him to the manor kitchens, delaying him ~15 minutes. Let slip that he came upriver from Marrowford the same day as Wren and "keeps an eye on the road for the steward."

time: 15 minutes later: Day 2, 6:07 PM

Tobin goes off like a startled hare, pelting for the kitchen yard, and you take the long way across the open green at an easy, unhurried pace, cutting the angle neatly. Your Deception check was a 20.

"Friend!" you call, warm as a hearth. "Forgive me, you look like a man who knows the way to the kitchens. I'm told there's supper for pilgrims."

The brown-coated man stops. His smile doesn't waver, but you see him weigh the thing, an honest pilgrim and a dozen eyes on the green. He lets the moment go. "Garrow, mistress. Hedge-carpenter, looking for work." He glances toward the gate, then back at you. "The kitchens are this way, aye. Round by the dovecote."

You walk him there, chatting the whole way about the Marrow's ferries, the price of bread, a pilgrim's blisters, and the smile slowly becomes a puzzled, polite thing. He lets slip that he came upriver from Marrowford the same day you did, and that he "keeps an eye on the road for the steward," then catches himself and laughs it off. By the time you reach the kitchen door, a quarter of an hour has gone, and Tobin has had all the time he needed.

The kitchen is warm, loud with pans and a spit turning over a fire. As you step in, a figure rises from a bench by the wall, neat and soft-voiced and smiling: Master Hale. He's holding a cup of cider as though he'd been there all evening.

"Mistress Ashgrove," he says pleasantly. "My lord is indisposed. He's asked not to be disturbed. Perhaps you'd care to sit and take supper with me, and we might talk like sensible people."

Behind him, through the passage, you can hear a door slam and a bolt shoot. That's Lord Edric's study, and Tobin got there first.

What does Wren do?

I give Hale my brightest grin and sit right down across from him, helping myself to a heel of bread. "Sensible people, Master Hale, my favourite kind. Let's talk, then: you tell me what you think I came here for, and I'll tell you whether you're warm or cold."

While he answers, I'll keep my hands in plain sight on the table and watch his eyes for what he reaches for first, the chest, the door, or his purse.

input.add_to_description: Day 2 evening in the Thornhallow kitchen: Hale offers Wren a "sensible" bargain: hand over Corvin's ledger from her road-psalter and he will see Lord Edric's charter "quietly made right" and pay her well. Reality: Hale has been Corvin's inside man in House Verrel for years, selling Corvin word of what clients can pay; he wants the ledger so no one can trace the forgeries or his share. Wren's natural-1 Insight misread him as bluffing and unsure what she carries; in fact Hale knows exactly that the ledger is hidden in the psalter's binding (Garrow saw it in Marrowford inn).

transcript.result: added to Master Hale's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Master Hale
time: 10 minutes later: Day 2, 6:17 PM

You sit and take the bread, and Hale folds his hands on the table with a look of mild, pleased attention. The cook clatters pans at the far end of the kitchen, out of hearing. Your Insight check was a natural 1, so what you read in him may well be wrong.

You think you see his eyes drift to the door and linger there, and his fingers twitch against his cup. To you he looks uncertain, like a man bluffing who isn't sure what you carry or what you know.

"Mistress Ashgrove," he says, gently. "I think you came to Thornhallow for the same reason as I did, to take care of my lord. I don't intend any harm to him or to you. Corvin Tallowmere's work has made a great many people comfortable. It would be a shame if it were... *disturbed*." He lets that sit. "I understand you carry something of his in your road-psalter. A book. If you let me look at it, I'll see that the charter is made right, quietly and kindly, without any assessor's help. And you would be well paid."

His smile never changes. He doesn't ask whether you have it. He just says where it is.

The smell of bread and onions fills the room, and the spit turns. Through the passage you hear nothing from Lord Edric's study. Tobin is behind that bolted door, and Garrow has slipped in by the dovecote entrance to stand near the pantry, not quite watching you.

What does Wren say or do?

I laugh softly and tear off a piece of bread. "Master Hale, you flatter me. The psalter's not on me, it's with a friend in Marrowford who has instructions to carry it straight to Dame Crowe if I'm not back to fetch it by noon on the day after tomorrow, so I'd think carefully about anything unkind happening to me or my lord's household." I smile sweetly. "Now, since we're being sensible, who exactly pays me well, you or whoever is paying you?"

input.add_to_description: Wren's Deception (8) failed to convince him her ledger is elsewhere. He pointed out that Garrow saw her put the psalter back in her pack at the Drowned Candle. He nodded to Garrow, who now stands at the kitchen's back door. Hale did not draw a weapon; he wants the book without scandal.

time: 2 minutes later: Day 2, 6:19 PM

You laugh, you spin it, and you ask your clever closing question. Your Deception check was an 8 against his sharpness, and it doesn't land.

Hale's smile doesn't change, but his eyes warm very slightly, the way a cat's might. "That's a lovely story, mistress. A friend in Marrowford." He takes a sip of cider. "I'd wager you've no friend in Marrowford at all. Garrow here saw you stow that psalter back in your pack at the Drowned Candle, and I rather think it hasn't left your side since." He doesn't look at Garrow, but he nods very slightly. By the back door, the carpenter shifts a pace to stand across the exit, hands loose, still wearing his easy smile.

"I don't want to hurt anyone," Hale says. "Truly. A book, a quiet word, and your road in the morning. My lord keeps his manor, you keep your head and a pouch of silver. The alternative is that the assessor arrives to find a girl who stole a ledger from a respected storyteller and bribed a country chaplain to counterfeit a register." He spreads his hands. "Which of us do you think she'd believe?"

The kitchen is warm, loud, ordinary, a cook with her back turned and a boy scraping pots. Nobody has drawn a weapon. The study's bolted door is thirty paces down the passage. Garrow is at the back door and Hale is across the table, calm, hands visible.

What does Wren do?

I stand up, push the stool back loudly, and pitch my voice to carry across the whole kitchen. "Master Hale, did I hear that right? You'll pay me a pouch of silver to hand over my lord's papers and be gone before the assessor comes?" I turn to the cook and the pot-boy with a bright, scandalized look. "Good people, you're all witnesses to the steward of Thornhallow offering a bribe to a pilgrim!"

Then I keep my hand off my rapier and walk steadily down the passage toward Lord Edric's study, calling, "My lord, it's Wren, open the door, the whole kitchen's heard your steward!"

The stool scrapes loudly and your voice rings across the kitchen like a bell. Your Performance check was a 12, just enough. The cook's ladle stops. The pot-boy's scraping stops. A kitchen-maid by the window turns with wide eyes, and every face in the room swings to Master Hale.

For the first time since you met him, the smile slips, only for a moment, a flicker of stone under the water. "A misunderstanding," Hale says evenly. "The pilgrim's overtired. I was merely..."

But the room has already decided. The cook folds her arms. The pot-boy mutters, "I heard 'silver,'" and nobody tells him to hush. Garrow, by the back door, shifts uneasily and glances at his master, and he doesn't step to block you. He can't do it in front of twelve pairs of eyes.

You walk down the passage steadily, hand well clear of the rapier, calling Lord Edric's name. Behind you Hale's chair scrapes and his soft, even footsteps follow at a polite distance. You reach the study door and hear the bolt rasp. It swings open an inch, then wide, and Tobin's pale face appears, and behind him Lord Edric stands with the key chain clutched at his neck.

"Child?" he says. "What is it? What did they hear?"

Hale arrives at your shoulder, composed again, hands folded. "My lord," he says quietly, "the girl has been telling tales in the kitchens. I thought it best to attend you."

The room is quiet. You hold the copy of the register entry and Osric's promise, and Lord Edric is looking from one of you to the other. What does Wren say or do?

I step inside and put the register copy straight into Lord Edric's hands, then stay between him and Hale. "My lord, read this first. Your grandsire Aldous married Maud Fenn, a miller's daughter, in your own chapel, and Brother Osric will swear to it before Dame Crowe. The land is yours by plain deed, and the Aldermere line was Corvin's invention."

I turn to Hale with a bright smile. "And while you read, my lord, ask your steward why he wanted the book in my psalter, and why a man who 'merely attends' brought a hedge-carpenter named Garrow from Marrowford."

input.add_to_description: Day 2 evening: read the register copy, accepted that the land is his by plain deed and the Aldermere line was invented. Ordered Hale to stay in the study while Edric questions him. Hale, cornered, said Wren stole Corvin's ledger and that he's been "protecting" the house from her. Edric now looks to Wren to explain the ledger.

time: 10 minutes later: Day 2, 6:34 PM

Lord Edric takes the sheet with both hands and reads it standing by the window, lips moving. Twice he stops, then goes back to the top. When he looks up his face has changed. It isn't the grey, hunted look any more, but something older and quieter.

"Aldous married Maud Fenn," he says. "My grandmother. I remember her hands. She smelled of flour." He laughs, a short, wet, startled sound. "I was ashamed of nothing. And Corvin sold me a shame to carry." He lowers the paper. "The land is mine by plain deed?"

"By a deed older than the charter, my lord. Osric will swear to it."

Then Lord Edric turns to Hale, who hasn't moved from your shoulder, and for the first time the steward's smile has gone entirely. In its place is an expression you can't read, a flat, thoughtful look.

"Hale. The book in her psalter. The man Garrow."

Hale lets out a slow breath. "My lord," he says quietly, "I'll be plain, since the girl has made plainness fashionable. Corvin Tallowmere's ledger is a record of the forgeries he sold to three houses. It would ruin Verrel in the right hands, and Dame Crowe's would be the right hands. This girl stole it from her master and has carried it here. I have been trying, for your sake, to take it from a thief and burn it before it harmed you." His eyes slide to you. "Ask her if it's true that she took it. Ask her what she means to do with it."

Tobin makes a small, frightened sound by the hearth. The kitchen has gathered quietly in the passage, listening. Lord Edric looks at you, and his voice is gentle, almost afraid. "Child. Is it so? Do you have Corvin's ledger?"

The lie that would be easiest isn't what any of them are waiting for. What does Wren say or do?

"Yes, my lord, I have it, and I'll not lie to you about that." I take the psalter from my pack, work the binding open, and slide out only the Verrel pages. "I took the ledger because I couldn't stomach what Corvin had done, and I came to find the people he'd cheated. This is your house's page. Burn it in the hearth, my lord, in front of everyone, because it's yours to burn, not Hale's."

I close the psalter again and look at Hale. "The other pages belong to two other houses, and I'll decide what's right for them myself, not by a steward's say-so. But I notice he wanted it burned *before* you saw it, and you're the one it concerns."

You don't flinch. You take out the psalter, work the stitched binding open with a thumbnail, and slide free a single folded leaf, then close the book again in plain view of the whole passage. The room stays utterly still.

"This is your house's page, my lord. It's yours to burn, not Hale's."

Lord Edric unfolds it. Corvin's neat hand lists dates, the sum paid and the descent altered. In the margin, in a smaller and different ink, run neat little initials and tallies: *H. — 2s. in the pound.* He reads them through, and you watch his shoulders go slowly straight.

"Two shillings in the pound," he says. "Out of my own purse."

He crosses to the hearth and drops the page onto the coals. It curls, browns, blooms briefly orange, and is gone. No one speaks. Then he turns to the doorway. "Master Hale will wait in the cellar store with the gate-guard at the door until the assessor comes. Nobody will lay a hand on him. Nobody will leave him without bread and water." His voice cracks only a little. "Take him."

Hale goes without a word, the smile folded away like a handkerchief. In the confusion Garrow is gone, over the dovecote wall into the dusk. Tobin thinks he went toward the Marrowford road, probably to carry word upriver to Corvin.

Lord Edric sits down heavily. He looks at you for a long time. "I'll tell Dame Crowe the plain truth," he says, "with Osric's name beside mine. If I lose the precedence, I lose it. A miller's granddaughter's bread was never a shameful thing." Then, softly: "What do I owe you, child?"

You have gained 100 XP, bringing you to 100 of 300. It's a quarter past seven on Day 2. Corvin is somewhere upriver and may learn that his forgery has failed, and two other houses in your psalter are still owed the truth.

What does Wren do?

I shake my head with a crooked smile. "Nothing, my lord, but a bed for the night, a hot supper, and two promises: that you'll keep Osric safe until the assessor comes, and that if a storyteller named Corvin shows up here, you'll send word to me before you open the door." I glance at the psalter in my hands. "The other two houses in this book are next, and I'd like to know their names and where they hold, so I'll sleep, then start on them at first light."

Lord Edric stares, then laughs shakily. "A bed, a supper, and two promises. Child, I'd have given you the south field." But he gives his word on both, hand on the table. Osric will be fetched to the manor under guard that very night, and if a storyteller named Corvin comes to the gate, a rider will find you before the door opens.

Supper is mutton and barley bread and a cup of cider, eaten at the kitchen table among cooks who now treat you like a visiting saint, or perhaps like a small, dangerous animal. Tobin sits at your elbow and doesn't say much, but he keeps pushing the best bits of the mutton toward you. He's asleep on a bench before the cider is gone. You're given a clean bed in a small room under the eaves.

Before sleeping you spread the two remaining leaves under a candle. The names are there in Corvin's neat hand. Lady Maren Thistlewood of Ashby Weir, two days upriver of Marrowford, was sold a hero's tale of an ancestor who held the ford, to claim ferry-toll rights. Sir Corwen Dray of Saltmarsh Keep, out on the estuary some three days downriver of here, bought a betrothal contract and a vow-tale tying his heir to a wealthy merchant family, and those merchants have begun to doubt. Both pages are struck through as paid. Corvin meant to mend only Verrel.

You sleep, and the night is quiet. It's just before seven now on Day 3, with the sun rising over a clean, cold morning. The assessor arrives tomorrow at noon. Corvin is somewhere upriver, and Garrow has had most of a night's start toward him.

What does Wren do?

I pack my psalter, thank the kitchen for the mutton, and find Lord Edric before breakfast. "My lord, lend me a mule and a short letter in your hand saying I act with your blessing. I'm going upriver through Marrowford to Lady Thistlewood at Ashby Weir, because that's where Corvin will be heading once Garrow finds him, and I'd rather meet him on my road than on his." On my way out I give Tobin a wink and slip him the last of my bread. "Keep your head down, Tobin, and if Osric needs anything, you're his legs."

A fishwife reports Garrow (brown coat) arrived at dawn on a lathered horse, spoke to the driver, and the wagon left at once north-upriver on the Ashby road with the driver whipping the team. Strongbox and everything went with it.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Corvin's Wagon
time: 6 hours 30 minutes later: Day 3, 1:29 PM

Lord Edric is at the kitchen table in his shirt-sleeves with a bowl of porridge, looking ten years younger. He hears you through, nods, and writes the letter himself with an ink-stained thumb and a flourish, sealing it with his signet in green wax. "To all whom it concerns: the bearer, Wren Ashgrove, acts with my full blessing and my gratitude." He also has the stable-boy saddle a placid grey mule called Biscuit.

Tobin takes the last of your bread with both hands, as if it were a medal, and nods fiercely. "I'll be Brother Osric's legs. I promise." Then, lower: "Thank you. For not being smiling."

You ride out of the gate into the cold bright morning with the Marrow glinting at your left hand. The road upriver is the same one you walked down, but it looks different under a mule's nodding head, wide and ordinary and slow. By half past one you're clattering over the stone bridge into Marrowford.

The square is busy with market-day trade, but your eye goes at once to the far corner. The place where Corvin's painted wagon stood is empty, with only a scatter of straw and a dark patch of oil on the cobbles. A fishwife by the tailor's stall sees you looking and wipes her hands. "Looking for the shrine-wagon, love? Gone at dawn. A man in a brown coat came in on a lathered horse, shouted at the driver, and off they went up the Ashby road like the river was on fire." She sniffs. "Strongbox and all."

So Garrow got word and the wagon moved, and the wagon is now on the road to Ashby Weir, the same road you meant to take, an hour or two of start ahead of you and a team of horses to your mule. It's half past one on Day 3.

What does Wren do?

I toss the fishwife a copper and lean down from Biscuit's back. "Thank you, love. Was Corvin himself aboard, or only the driver and the man in the brown coat, and did either of them ask after a young woman with a lute?" Then I turn the mule toward the Ashby road, keeping to a steady walk so I don't spend him, and think it over as I go: the wagon is hours ahead, so I'd rather arrive after them and watch Lady Thistlewood's gate than ride in on their heels.

Run by a lay-keeper named Marta Pell, a cheerful widow. Offers free bed and bread to Lantern-Bearer faithful (Wren's Shelter of the Faithful).

You flip her a copper and she snatches it neatly out of the air. "Only the driver and the brown-coated one," she says. "Not the master, not that I saw. The brown coat asked the stall-folk whether a young half-elf with a lute had come through, and he wasn't sweet about it. Sharp-faced fellow. Take care, love."

You have 14 gp 6 sp 1 cp now, down a copper. And the tinker, if you ask, still wants his 25 gp for the thieves' tools. He hasn't moved his tray, and it's the same price, so it's out of reach for now.

You turn Biscuit up the Ashby road at an easy walk and let the afternoon pass. The road climbs away from the river, runs through hop fields, then oak woods, then open heath. You keep the pace steady and the mule unhurried, watching for dust or wheel-ruts. About half past six, with the sky going the colour of a bruise, a thin thread of smoke and a small glowing lamp appear ahead where the road forks.

It's a squat stone shrine-house with a tiled roof and a lantern hung on a pole by its door, a brass lamp with rays carved into the shutters, the Lantern-Bearer's sign. A hand-painted board by the gate says **LANTERN'S REST: BED, BREAD, AND A LIGHT FOR ANY WHO WALK.** A plump, grey-haired woman in a green apron is raking the yard and looks up as you approach.

There are fresh wheel-ruts in the soft ground by the gate, two wheels, heavy, turned in and out. Wagon ruts, and recent.

What does Wren do?

I dismount, pat Biscuit's neck, and walk up with the reliquary held openly in my palm so the lamp catches its brass. "Evening, Mother. A traveler of the Lantern-Bearer asks shelter for herself and a mule, and if you've bread to spare, I'd be glad of it." Then, glancing at the ruts, lightly: "Looks like a wagon came through ahead of me. Did a shrine-wagon stop here, and did its driver say where they'd sleep?"

The woman's face crinkles into a smile at the sight of the little brass lantern. "Bless me, a real one! Marta Pell, keeper here these fourteen years. Come in, love, come in. There's a bunk and a bowl of barley broth and your mule can have the lean-to." She takes Biscuit's rein herself and clucks at him like an old friend. The bed and the bread are free, as the shrine's custom is for any of the faithful.

As she leads the mule round the side, she answers you without needing to be asked twice. The wagon came through at noon, painted lantern and all, with a brown-coated man shouting at the driver. "But Master Tallowmere was already here. He's lodged with me the night before, the dear man, and he's been coming through these seven years. He gave that lamp over the door." She nods to the brass lantern. "He said he'd a lady to see about a ford, up at Ashby Weir, and took the wagon straight on. Left in a great hurry, the brown one in a terrible taking."

She stops, wipes her hands on her apron, and fishes in a pocket. "And he left this for a young woman with a lute, if she should come by. 'Tall, half-elf, quick with a smile,' he said. I thought you'd be her the moment you rode up." She pushes a small, folded square of vellum into your hand, sealed with a blob of blue wax and the shrine-lantern stamped on it.

Inside, a fire crackles in the hearth, and the smell of barley broth drifts out. Corvin knew you were coming, or guessed. He stayed one step ahead of you here.

You can open the note now, take a moment with Marta first, or sleep on it. What does Wren do?

I check the seal carefully under the lamp for signs of tampering or anything odd, like a pin-prick, powder or a trap, then break the wax and read it by the lantern's light. Whatever it says, I'll keep my face still, because Marta's watching and I'd like to hear it from my own head first.

You rest him at noon by a trough, and the afternoon lengthens. If someone is watching from the copses, you wouldn't know it.

By five in the evening the road tops a low rise and the land opens. Below lies Ashby Weir. A long, low stone weir holds back a pale gleam of river, and downstream of it the ford spreads wide and shallow, studded with stepping stones. A cluster of thatched cottages leans along the bank, with smoke rising from them and a larger inn, the Heron and Net, at the centre. Upstream, a grey manor house stands on a spur among willows, the Thistlewood seat. Nearer, at the water's edge by the ford, a small crooked cottage with a green door sits beside a heap of lobster pots and a drying rack of nets.

There's no wagon in sight. There's no sign of Corvin. The ford is two days of walking from Marrowford, and you've made it with a day to spare. Dusk is two hours away.

You tie Biscuit among the lobster pots and knock on the green door. Nothing, then a shuffle, then the bolt. The door opens a hand's width on a face like a dried apple, with white whiskers and bright, watery eyes. "Who's that? Is it the tax-man?"

"A traveler of the Lantern-Bearer, sent by Mother Pell, who says you keep the best memory on the river." You hold up the reliquary so the dying sun catches its rays, and then the sketch. Your Persuasion check was a 13, and the eyes sharpen.

"The crooked flame," he whispers. The door opens, and he draws you into a smoky room that smells of tar and pipe-weed. He sits you by the hearth and takes the sketch in a shaking hand, and for a moment you think his wits have drifted off. Then they come back like a boat on a tide.

"Elowen," he says. "Elowen Ashgrove. A road-priest of the Lantern, proper, with a lamp-staff and a looped hand. She came through the shrine twenty years back with a babe wrapped in a green blanket, hungry and cold, and she asked me to cut the book's pages for that season. I said it was a sin, and she said it was a mercy. So I did, with her own knife." He wipes his eye. "She left the lamp over the door, and a curl of blessing in a little brass case, and said she was going upriver to Ashby Weir, to a house she trusted. And that was the last of her. I never saw her again."

His gaze settles on your face for a long moment. "A storyteller came asking after her the next spring. Silver-tongued. Too many questions. I told him nothing, and he went off sulking. That would have been your Master Tallowmere, would it?"

He says her surname the same way the world has said yours since you were small. *Ashgrove.* You have no memory of a name before it, and the old man is watching your face for what you'll do with it.

Dusk is over an hour away. You could ask him what house she trusted, what became of the baby, or who else knew. What does Wren do?

My voice comes out smaller than I mean it to, and I hold the reliquary a little tighter. "Master Crannock, which house did she trust? Was it the Thistlewoods up on the spur, and the babe in the green blanket... was there a ribbon with it, green velvet?" I take the scrap from my cloak hem and lay it on his knee. "Please, take your time. I'd rather have it slow and true than quick."

You lay the scrap of green velvet on his knee and tell him to take his time. The old man doesn't touch it at first. He looks at it for a long while with his mouth working, and the fire pops, and a gull cries on the weir. You wait.

"Green velvet," he says at last, very softly. "Aye. The blanket was edged in it, deep as moss, a good bolt, a noble's cloth. It was too fine for a priest's baby. I remember thinking that." He lifts the scrap with one thumb and forefinger as if it might bruise. "She said she was going to the lady on the spur. Old Lady Agnes Thistlewood, the grandmother of the house, may she rest. She was kind. Good to the road. Elowen said, 'Agnes will keep her safe till I can come back.'" His voice thins. "But she never came back, as far as I ever heard, and I don't know what Lady Agnes did with the child. Only..."

He frowns, hunting for the thread. "Some months after, a storyteller came down the Marrowford road with a little girl of about that age on his cart. Said he found her at a roadside shrine, wrapped in a blanket. Pretty talker. I thought nothing of it then." He looks up at you and doesn't say the rest, because he doesn't need to.

"Lady Maren rules the spur now, her daughter," he adds. "A fair woman, but afraid of the village over the ferry-toll, and not much liked. She was only a girl herself then. She might remember, or she might not."

The fire burns low. Outside, the light has turned gold and slanting over the ford. It's ten past six, and dusk is an hour away. Corvin's meeting is tomorrow at dusk, and the Thistlewood house is on the spur above the village.

I thank Hob warmly, tuck the scrap of velvet back into my hem, and ask him one more thing: whether he'd be willing to speak for Elowen's mark if a lady asked him. Then I ride Biscuit up the spur to the Thistlewood gate, with Lord Edric's sealed letter in hand and the psalter pages for Lady Maren's house at the ready, and ask to see her tonight on a matter of her family's honor and her mother's kindness to a road-priest.

Hob nods, slow and certain. "If a lady asks me, I'll say what I saw, and swear it on Elowen's lamp. I owe her that." He walks you to the green door and watches you go.

The spur path winds up through willows, and Biscuit takes it without complaint. The gatehouse of the Thistlewood manor is shut for the evening. A pair of tired-looking men-at-arms in faded blue peer down at you, and your Persuasion check was a 13. Lord Edric's green-waxed letter does most of the work, passed up on the point of a halberd and carried inside. You wait with the mule among the cooling stones while the dusk gathers, and a bat flits over the wall. Then the wicket opens.

You're led across a small, worn courtyard into a long, panelled hall, hung with faded banners and a single great painting of a stern man at a ford, with the river gleaming behind him, the hero of Corvin's tale, you realise. At the far end, by a fire too large for the room's warmth, sits a straight-backed woman in her forties in a grey gown, with ink-stained fingers and a worn expression of guarded politeness. This is Lady Maren Thistlewood.

She has your letter open on her knee. "Lord Edric Verrel writes that the bearer acts with his blessing," she says. "He doesn't say why. I'm told you spoke of my mother's kindness to a road-priest." Her gaze is steady, a little tired. "I'm not often visited by anyone at this hour who isn't asking for the toll. Sit, Mistress Ashgrove. I'd like to hear what you have to say."

You have the ledger pages in your psalter, Hob's story, and Corvin's note. Corvin himself meets you tomorrow at dusk. Somewhere out in the dark Garrow's eyes may be on you.

What does Wren say?

I sit, keep my hands visible, and tell her plainly. "My lady, I'm a storyteller's apprentice, and I've come to give you the truth about the hero at the ford in that painting: Corvin Tallowmere sold your family a tale, and I have his own page recording the sale." I place the Thistlewood leaf on the arm of her chair, then add more gently, "And a second matter, if you'll allow it: your mother once took in a road-priest called Elowen Ashgrove, with a babe wrapped in green velvet. I think that babe grew up to sit before you."

She reads the leaf by the firelight, once, then again, her ink-stained thumb moving along Corvin's neat hand. When she looks up there isn't surprise in her face, only a deep weariness, as of a debt long expected. "I wondered," she says. "I'd sit under that painting and think, no man ever looked so tidy in a river." She folds the leaf and holds it as if it weighed a great deal. "The ford tale held for twenty years because no one dared look. Now the village will."

Then your second matter lands, and the weariness changes into something stranger. She is quiet for a long time. She looks at your face, your eyes, the way you hold your hands.

"I was twenty-four when she came," she says. "A road-priest, thin as a heron, with a baby in a blanket the colour of a forest. My mother was sick that year, and she took them in without a question. The child slept in my own old cradle by that fire for three months, until the road-priest went out one evening and didn't come back." Her voice catches. "Then a man arrived, a storyteller, charming, silver-tongued, with a letter in the priest's hand asking for the child to be given to him. My mother was ill and she believed it. She gave him the baby, and the key to a coffer the priest had left behind 'for the girl when she's grown.' I watched him ride away with her." She presses her lips together. She rises. "The coffer is still here. Mother wouldn't send it away, and the key went with the storyteller. Come."

She leads you down a stair to a small stone strongroom, and by the light of her candle you see it on a shelf: a little iron-bound coffer scratched with a lantern and the letters *E.A.* It is no bigger than a bread-box. Locked.

You've heard Corvin's name linked to this twice in a day. He has the key, and he'll be at the ford at dusk tomorrow.

The lid rises. Inside, on a bed of faded green velvet, lie three things: a small silver pendant shaped like a lantern, a folded paper sealed with plain wax and marked with a lamp-staff, and a single letter in a looped hand you know from the parchment in your reliquary. You read it kneeling, with a hand over your mouth. It isn't long. Elowen writes that Corvin Tallowmere was her own apprentice, that he turned her blessings into pedigrees and sold the road's mercy to men who wanted it for their vanity, and that she meant to confront him. If she did not return, she wrote, he would come for the child with false letters and a pleasant face. *Light the road, don't sell it. The folded paper is a commission, naming you heir to her lamp-staff and her calling, if you want it.

You've gained the letter, the pendant, and the commission, and learned more than you came for. It's ten past eight on Day 4. Corvin is a day's wait away at the ford, and he knows it is true.

RULE Dropping to 0 Hit Points:
When you drop to 0 hit points, you either die outright or fall unconscious, as explained in the following sections.

#### Instant Death

Massive damage can kill you instantly. When damage reduces you to 0 hit points and there is damage remaining, you die if the remaining damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum.

For example, a cleric with a maximum of 12 hit points currently has 6 hit points. If she takes 18 damage from an attack, she is reduced to 0 hit points, but 12 damage remains. Because the remaining damage equals her hit point maximum, the cleric dies.

#### Falling Unconscious

If damage reduces you to 0 hit points and fails to kill you, you fall unconscious (see appendix PH-A). This unconsciousness ends if you regain any hit points.

#### Death Saving Throws

Whenever you start your turn with 0 hit points, you must make a special saving throw, called a death saving throw, to determine whether you creep closer to death or hang onto life. Unlike other saving throws, this one isn't tied to any ability score. You are in the hands of fate now, aided only by spells and features that improve your chances of succeeding on a saving throw.

Roll a d20. If the roll is 10 or higher, you succeed. Otherwise, you fail. A success or failure has no effect by itself. On your third success, you become stable (see below). On your third failure, you die. The successes and failures don't need to be consecutive; keep track of both until you collect three of a kind. The number of both is reset to zero when you regain any hit points or become stable.

***Rolling 1 or 20.*** When you make a death saving throw and roll a 1 on the d20, it counts as two failures. If you roll a 20 on the d20, you regain 1 hit point.

***Damage at 0 Hit Points.*** If you take any damage while you have 0 hit points, you suffer a death saving throw failure. If the damage is from a critical hit, you suffer two failures instead. If the damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum, you suffer instant death.

#### Stabilizing a Creature

The best way to save a creature with 0 hit points is to heal it. If healing is unavailable, the creature can at least be stabilized so that it isn't killed by a failed death saving throw.

You can use your action to administer first aid to an unconscious creature and attempt to stabilize it, which requires a successful DC 10 Wisdom (Medicine) check.

A **stable** creature doesn't make death saving throws, even though it has 0 hit points, but it does remain unconscious. The creature stops being stable, and must start making death saving throws again, if it takes any damage. A stable creature that isn't healed regains 1 hit point after 1d4 hours.

#### Monsters and Death

Most GMs have a monster die the instant it drops to 0 hit points, rather than having it fall unconscious and make death saving throws.

Mighty villains and special nonplayer characters are common exceptions; the GM might have them fall unconscious and follow the same rules as player characters.

The rapier's point had barely touched his collar when Corvin's eyes flicked over your shoulder. Your Intimidation check was a 3, and the driver took no heed of it. You see Corvin's mouth begin to curve, and he says nothing. He doesn't give the order. The bolt strikes before you can turn.

It's a critical hit. Eleven points of damage drop you off the stone and into the cold ford, and the world goes grey at the edges. You hear shouting, the splash of boots, water in your ears. One bolt more flies past you and misses. Then Alder's spear goes wide, and Kit's finds the driver, and he folds beside Garrow in the shallows.

You lie at the bottom of the dark. Twice you hear Alder's voice and Hob's wheeze over you, hands pressing at your wound and failing, and Kit swearing in a language you don't know. You make your death saves in the dark, one ten, then a thirteen before it, and the next round something bright and fierce answers in you: a natural 20. You come up gasping into the lamplight with one hit point and a mouthful of river.

Corvin is gone. When you turn your head, the flat stone is empty, a wet footprint drying on it. One of the wagon's horses is missing from the picket line, and the dusk has swallowed him. The wagon stands on the bank with its painted lantern, abandoned, and the strongbox sits on its tailboard, still locked.

You are alive. It's nearly six now, on Day 5. You're at 1 hit point, 1 spell slot left, and 225 XP, 75 short of the next level. I gave you 50 XP for the fight. Garrow and the driver are dead, and the villagers are gathered quietly on the bank, looking at you with a different face than they wore at noon. Lady Maren is hurrying down from the spur.

Corvin said "Saltmarsh," and you still have the ledger in your psalter, two leaves for Thistlewood and Dray, and a night of rest ahead.

What does Wren do?

I let Alder and Kit haul me onto the bank, cough up half the river, and manage a croaky "Thank you, both, and you, Hob." Then I ask Lady Maren for a bed, and while I'm lying propped up I send Kit to search the driver's belt and pockets for the strongbox key, and Hob to keep an eye on the wagon until morning.

"In the morning," I add weakly, "I'm opening that strongbox, and then I'm riding for Saltmarsh."

Alder and Kit haul you up the bank like a netted fish, and you cough up what feels like half the Marrow. You manage a croaky "Thank you, both, and you, Hob," and Hob only snorts around his pipe, wiping his eyes with a knuckle. Lady Maren arrives at a run with a lantern and a blanket, takes one look at you, and says nothing at all for a moment. Then she orders a litter.

Before they carry you off, you send Kit to the driver, and he comes back with a dead man's belt-pouch. Inside is a small iron key, a few coppers, and a scrap of vellum folded small. Hob takes the wagon watch with a rug over his knees and his pipe, and Alder stays at his side.

You sleep in the same small room under the eaves, in a clean bed with a jug of water and a heel of bread. It's a long, heavy sleep, and when you wake the window is full of white morning. You're whole again: all your hit points and your spell slots, and Bardic Inspiration back at three. The night has passed without trouble.

At seven you go down to the yard with Kit. The wagon stands by the tithe-barn, its painted lantern faded in the daylight, and the strongbox sits on its tailboard. The little iron key fits. Inside, packed in straw, lie a good set of lock-picks and tools, a full forgery kit in a lacquered case, a purse of sixty gold pieces in mixed coin, and one slip of paper in Corvin's neat hand: *The Salt Gull, Saltmarsh, the ninth.*

That's Day 9. You've pocketed the money, the kit and the tools, and the note. The tools you wanted at the tinker's are now yours, 74 gold and some silver in all.

Lady Maren stands at your elbow, her hands clasped. "The village is quiet this morning," she says. "They saw you take a bolt for the truth. I think they'll listen now." She hesitates. "Will you ride for Saltmarsh? Sir Corwen Dray is a hard man, I hear, and proud. You'll want something to carry in front of you."

You have three days before the ninth. Saltmarsh is some five days' ride by the river road, so you won't make it by Day 9 without hard riding and a lucky road. You're at 225 XP, 75 short of level 2.

What does Wren do?

"I'll ride for Saltmarsh, my lady, and I'll have to ride hard to make the ninth." I tuck the thieves' tools and forgery kit into my pack, and for once I keep the forgery kit for honest work. "If you can spare a swift horse in place of Biscuit, and a letter under your own seal naming me your friend and Elowen Ashgrove's daughter, it'll open doors in Saltmarsh that Lord Edric's letter won't."

I turn to Kit with a grin. "And if Alder can spare you for a week, I'd gladly buy your spear on the road, a lady needs a second pair of eyes when she's chasing a man who nearly watched her die."

Lady Maren doesn't answer at once. She looks at the wagon, at the faded lantern, at Alder leaning on his spear, and then at you. "A horse, yes. My father's grey, Ember, who's too good for this village and bored with it. And a letter." She goes into the manor and returns within a quarter of an hour with a sealed square of vellum, and she hands it over with both hands, as if it were heavier than it looked. She has written it in her own square hand, naming you her friend and Elowen Ashgrove's daughter, "with every claim on the house of Thistlewood that her mother had, and gladly given."

Biscuit goes back to the stable with the promise that Lord Edric's stable-boy will fetch him when the dust settles. Ember is a tall grey with a white blaze and an opinion of himself, and he regards you the way a cat regards a puddle.

Then she turns to Kit. "I'll not order it. I'll ask." Kit says nothing for a moment, one thumb in her sword-belt. She looks at the wagon, at the ford, at you. "Aye," she says at last. "I've never been past the weir. Time I saw where the river goes." Alder claps her on the shoulder, and Lady Maren pays her a month's wage in advance without being asked. Kit stows her shield on her back, shoulders a pack, and gives you a brief, dry nod, no speech.

Kit is a human fighter, a solid companion with chain mail, a shield, a longsword, a light crossbow and a steady head. She has her own character sheet now and takes her turns as herself in a fight, on your orders if you give them.

It's quarter to eight on Day 6. Saltmarsh is days away, and the Salt Gull meeting is on Day 9. The river road runs down past Marrowford and Thornhallow, and you can leave now, or stop on the way.

What does Wren do?

"Then let's ride, Kit. You take the first watch tonight and I'll take the second, and I'll teach you a song to pass the miles." I swing up onto Ember, who snorts at me in disdain, and pat his neck. RULE Speed:
Every character and monster has a speed, which is the distance in feet that the character or monster can walk in 1 round. This number assumes short bursts of energetic movement in the midst of a life-threatening situation.

The following rules determine how far a character or monster can move in a minute, an hour, or a day.

#### Travel Pace

While traveling, a group of adventurers can move at a normal, fast, or slow pace, as shown on the Travel Pace table. The table states how far the party can move in a period of time and whether the pace has any effect. A fast pace makes characters less perceptive, while a slow pace makes it possible to sneak around and to search an area more carefully.

***Forced March.*** The Travel Pace table assumes that characters travel for 8 hours in day. They can push on beyond that limit, at the risk of exhaustion.

For each additional hour of travel beyond 8 hours, the characters cover the distance shown in the Hour column for their pace, and each character must make a Constitution saving throw at the end of the hour. The DC is 10 + 1 for each hour past 8 hours. On a failed saving throw, a character suffers one level of exhaustion (see appendix PH-A).

***Mounts and Vehicles.*** For short spans of time (up to an hour), many animals move much faster than humanoids. A mounted character can ride at a gallop for about an hour, covering twice the usual distance for a fast pace. If fresh mounts are available every 8 to 10 miles, characters can cover larger distances at this pace, but this is very rare except in densely populated areas.

Characters in wagons, carriages, or other land vehicles choose a pace as normal. Characters in a waterborne vessel are limited to the speed of the vessel, and they don't suffer penalties for a fast pace or gain benefits from a slow pace. Depending on the vessel and the size of the crew, ships might be able to travel for up to 24 hours per day.

Certain special mounts, such as a pegasus or griffon, or special vehicles, such as a *carpet of flying*, allow you to travel more swiftly.

#### Difficult Terrain

The travel speeds given in the Travel Pace table assume relatively simple terrain: roads, open plains, or clear dungeon corridors. But adventurers often face dense forests, deep swamps, rubble-filled ruins, steep mountains, and ice-covered ground-all considered difficult terrain.

You keep your voice low and plain, and you lay the Thistlewood letter in her hand with the coins beside it. Bess reads the seal, and for a breath something moves behind her eyes. Your Persuasion check was a 9 with disadvantage, and it isn't enough.

She pushes the gold back at you without counting it. "No." The word is quiet and tired. "He pays for this roof, and for my silence, and he's a man who remembers who talks. I'll not say who's in that room or how many." She hesitates, then adds, grimly, almost against her will, "I'll say the wedding folk at the hall will be done by noon. After that I can't say what comes down my stair."

She isn't a villain. She's frightened, and she's given you the one thing she can: the hour. It's twenty past ten. At noon the contract is sealed, and whoever is behind the brass lock has until then to be somewhere else.

Down on the quay, Kit is a blue spot at the edge of the crowd before the Vantry hall. The clerk with the case has gone inside.

I scoop the coins back with a nod of thanks and leave Bess be, then slip into the alley by the stairs and cast Disguise Self, making myself a tidy, ink-stained notary's junior with a wax-tablet satchel and a sober face. description.text: River-market town built around a stone bridge and a lantern-hung market square. Busy at dusk as stalls close and lamps are lit.
Wren's mentor, a caravan storyteller and forger of tales sold to nobles. Worships the Lantern-Bearer only as cover. Wren stole his ledger of forged tales.

Day 3: Corvin lodged at Lantern's Rest the night before and joined his wagon there at noon, charming the keeper Marta Pell. He left a sealed note for "a young woman with a lute" (Wren) in Marta's keeping, then took the wagon toward Ashby Weir with Garrow and the driver. He seems to have expected her.

Note to Wren (Day 3): affectionate, cool. Says she "took the wrong book" and that he is not angry; invites her to meet him at Ashby Weir's ford at dusk on Day 5 with the ledger, alone, "to talk like family." Adds that the curl of parchment in her reliquary is NOT his work: "I never wrote it. Ask yourself who did, and why I let you carry it all this way." Signed with a small drawn lantern.

Per Elowen's letter: was her apprentice, became a forger who sold her true blessings as noble pedigrees; she was going to confront him when she vanished. Whether he killed her or merely took the child is unknown. He fears the coffer and the true key; his note's "who wrote it" hinted at this.

Day 5: Corvin's people (Garrow, the driver) have already come to the ford before Wren's scouting; she failed Perception (6) and saw nothing. Wagon is hidden in a tithe-barn a quarter mile up the Ashby road.

Day 5 dusk, at the ford: walked out alone to Wren, a silver-haired man in his fifties with ink-black gloves and a warm, rueful voice. Wren's Insight (12) could not tell truth from lie. He claims: (1) he never harmed Elowen; she left him "to walk the road alone" and he took the child to keep her safe; (2) Elowen is alive and he knows where, so long as Wren hands over the ledger; (3) the Lantern's blessings are "just paper", but he has kept the faith in his own way; (4) he will burn the Thistlewood and Dray pages himself and make restitution if she gives him the book. Garrow waits at the wagon with the driver, who has a crossbow. Corvin keeps the decoy iron key on a cord at his neck.

Day 5 dusk: answered Wren's challenge by naming "Saltmarsh" as where Elowen is (the estuary town beneath Saltmarsh Keep, seat of House Dray; true or lie unknown). Then demanded the ledger "now", and signalled the driver (crossbow) and Garrow (short sword). Alder and Kit (Thistlewood men-at-arms) stepped out of the willows.

Day 5 dusk: the fight at the ford killed Garrow and the driver. Corvin vanished into the dusk during the fight, taking a wagon horse and leaving the wagon and strongbox. He named "Saltmarsh" as where Elowen is. He holds the decoy iron key. His whereabouts unknown; probably riding downriver toward Saltmarsh.

Caravan wagon painted with Corvin's shrine-lantern sigil, parked at the edge of Marrowford's square. Driver is a weathered, bored man. A locked iron-bound strongbox sits on the tailboard. No sign of Corvin.

Inside under the canvas: a folding travelling shrine of the Lantern-Bearer with a false back panel; behind it a flat leather case of blank vellum, seals-in-wax impressions (a Verrel seal among them), and a half-written draft letter in Corvin's hand, "to be mended before the assessor", with a list of three noble houses and sums owed. A sleeping cot, one cloak.

Day 3 ~1:30 PM: gone from Marrowford's square. A fishwife reports Garrow (brown coat) arrived at dawn on a lathered horse, spoke to the driver, and the wagon left at once north-upriver on the Ashby road with the driver whipping the team. Strongbox and everything went with it.
Day 5 dusk: abandoned on the Ashby road bank by the ford after the fight; one horse of the team missing. Strongbox still locked on the tailboard. In Lady Maren's custody.

Day 6 morning: strongbox opened with the driver's key by Wren. Contents: 60 gp in mixed coin, a good set of thieves' tools, a forgery kit, and a note in Corvin's hand: "The Salt Gull, Saltmarsh, the ninth." Wren took them; Lady Maren keeps the wagon until the dead men's kin are found.
Young page in minor noble's livery, pressing a sealed letter on the wagon's driver. The seal resembles one Wren saw in Corvin's ledger. Noble house not yet named.
Spotted Wren tailing him on the bridge. Boy of about fourteen, nervous, called Tobin; goes by Tobin Reed once he speaks.

Now trusts Wren somewhat. Tobin Reed, servant to Lord Edric. Knows the Verrel charter was bought from Corvin years ago and that Lord Edric is terrified. Lord Edric is sending him on to Thornhallow tonight; Tobin is lodging at the Drowned Candle inn in Marrowford.

Wren saw a page give a sealed letter bearing a seal from Corvin's ledger to the driver of his wagon in Marrowford. Find out what links the stolen ledger to this noble house, and decide whether to expose or fix it.

Overheard: page serves Lord Edric Verrel of Thornhallow; letter is for Corvin's hand only; an assessor comes to Thornhallow in three days to check the Verrel lineage charter. Driver says Corvin went upriver and will return in a day or two; he took the letter and a coin. Page left toward the bridge.

Tobin: charter is in a locked chest in Lord Edric's study at Thornhallow; Hale has a spare key. Lord Edric would likely trust Corvin's apprentice. Thornhallow is a day's walk downriver; the assessor comes in three days.

Day 2: Brother Osric's register shows the third descent's marriage was real but to Maud Fenn, miller's daughter, not an Aldermere. The Verrel claim to Aldermere blood is false; the manor itself is held by plain land-grant. Wren's reliquary parchment is a genuine blessing of the Lantern-Bearer. Hale tried to see the register and was refused.

Day 2 ~7 PM: Lord Edric burned the Verrel ledger page. Hale confined; Garrow fled toward Marrowford to warn Corvin. Remaining: Dame Crowe arrives noon Day 4 (Lord Edric to confess the plain truth with Osric's attestation); Corvin will return; two other houses in the ledger (names not yet read) are still owed truth or restitution.

Day 2 night: Wren read the two other pages. House Thistlewood (Lady Maren, Ashby Weir, two days upriver of Marrowford; forged ford/toll tale) and House Dray (Sir Corwen, Saltmarsh Keep, estuary three days downriver; forged betrothal contract). Both paid and "struck through" in Corvin's draft; Corvin planned to mend only Verrel.

Day 3 night: Corvin's note invites Wren alone to the ford at Ashby Weir at dusk on Day 5 with the ledger; claims the reliquary parchment isn't his. New thread: who wrote it and why Corvin let her keep it.

Minor river-farm noble house, seat at Thornhallow. Lord Edric Verrel bought a forged lineage tale from Corvin. His page is frightened because a royal assessor will verify the house's lineage charter in three days.

Thornhallow is a day's walk downriver from Marrowford by the river road. The lineage charter is kept in an iron-bound chest in Lord Edric's study; the key is on his neck-chain, but Master Hale keeps a copy. Lord Edric trusts only Corvin; years ago he saw a young girl with Corvin who sang for his table (Wren, possibly). Tobin can vouch for a stranger if she brings a token only Corvin's circle would know.

Lord Edric admits (Day 2): Corvin sold him the charter as a "restoration" from true records, and he has half-suspected the third descent (grandsire's marriage into the Aldermere line) might be false. Only Lord Edric, Corvin, Hale and the old chaplain Brother Osric have seen it. Hale keeps a spare key and has had it copied by a scribe in Marrowford. The royal assessor, a woman named Dame Ilsabet Crowe, arrives Day 4 at noon.

Charter examined by Wren (Day 2, Investigation 9): third descent is in a hand close to the others and aged with tea-wash, but she cannot tell whether the marriage itself was invented or merely its name. Needs Brother Osric's parish register in the Thornhallow chapel vestry. Brother Osric is old, half-deaf, and keeps the register in the chapel on the green at the edge of the village.

Day 7 at Thornhallow: Dame Crowe came Day 4, heard Lord Edric's confession and Osric's attestation. Ruling: the Aldermere precedence and tax-right are struck from the Verrel charter and a fine levied; the plain land-grant stands, so the manor is kept. Crowe wants Corvin Tallowmere and the ledger. Hale is held for the assessor's court. Tobin and Osric are safe.
Someone Tobin fears; Tobin thought Wren might be him or his agent. Role unknown; Tobin says Hale's people "smile too." Possibly the assessor's man, a creditor, or a rival of the Verrels.

Per Tobin: Hale is the Verrel household's steward-clerk who handles Lord Edric's money, a cold smiling man. He has been pressing Tobin to learn what Lord Edric sends to Corvin and to whom. Tobin suspects Hale means to sell the Verrel secret to the assessor's side, or to Lord Edric's rival, for gain.

Met Wren in Lord Edric's study at Thornhallow: neat, middle-aged, soft-voiced steward-clerk with a warm smile. Wren's Insight (21): the smile never changes, yet his eyes went to the iron chest when the ribbon was laid down and again to the door; he already knew Wren was coming and who she was ("the apprentice"). He is afraid of her, not for Lord Edric but for himself: he fears the ledger's truth coming out. Complied with Lord Edric's dismissal but slowly, and shut the door softly.

Day 2 evening in the Thornhallow kitchen: Hale offers Wren a "sensible" bargain: hand over Corvin's ledger from her road-psalter and he will see Lord Edric's charter "quietly made right" and pay her well. Reality: Hale has been Corvin's inside man in House Verrel for years, selling Corvin word of what clients can pay; he wants the ledger so no one can trace the forgeries or his share. Wren's natural-1 Insight misread him as bluffing and unsure what she carries; in fact Hale knows exactly that the ledger is hidden in the psalter's binding (Garrow saw it in Marrowford inn).

Wren's Deception (8) failed to convince him her ledger is elsewhere. He pointed out that Garrow saw her put the psalter back in her pack at the Drowned Candle. He nodded to Garrow, who now stands at the kitchen's back door. Hale did not draw a weapon; he wants the book without scandal.

Publicly exposed in the kitchen at Thornhallow (Day 2, ~6:25 PM) by Wren's Performance (12): the cook, a pot-boy and a kitchen-maid heard him offer a pouch of silver to Wren to hand over "my lord's papers" and leave before the assessor came. Hale denied it with perfect calm ("a misunderstanding"), but he cannot now act openly in front of the household.

Day 2 ~7 PM: Verrel ledger page bore Hale's marginal initials and sums, his cut as Corvin's informant inside the house. Lord Edric burned the page himself in the study hearth, then had Hale locked in the cellar store under guard of the old gate-guard until the assessor comes. Garrow slipped over the wall in the confusion and fled upriver toward Marrowford, presumably to warn Corvin.

Deep green velvet ribbon Lord Edric Verrel gave Wren as a child after she sang at his table in Thornhallow. Corvin pocketed the ribbon; Wren kept a scrap sewn into her old caravan cloak's hem. Possible token to win Lord Edric's trust.

Unnamed lean man in a tradesman's brown coat, one of Master Hale's agents. Wren rolled a natural 1 on Perception on the river road and did not notice him. He followed her out of Marrowford, having seen her speak with Tobin on the bridge, and will track her to Thornhallow.
Day 2, 5:50 PM: Wren spotted him by the village well on the green, brown tradesman's coat; he turned toward the manor gate when she left the chapel, evidently to report to Hale.

Gave his name as Garrow, a "hedge-carpenter looking for work", when Wren (Deception 20) walked him to the manor kitchens, delaying him ~15 minutes. Let slip that he came upriver from Marrowford the same day as Wren and "keeps an eye on the road for the steward."

Day 4: Wren failed Perception (3) on the Ashby road and did not see Garrow shadowing her from the heath/copses, hat low. He reports to Corvin's camp near Ashby Weir. He now knows she is going to the ford.
Died at the ford at Ashby Weir, Day 5, speared by Kit (Thistlewood man-at-arms) while attacking Wren.

Master of Thornhallow, minor noble, sleepless and frightened about the assessor's inspection of his lineage charter. Wept when Wren, as a child, sang at his table and gave her a green velvet ribbon. Trusts only Corvin.

Day 2 evening: read the register copy, accepted that the land is his by plain deed and the Aldermere line was invented. Ordered Hale to stay in the study while Edric questions him. Hale, cornered, said Wren stole Corvin's ledger and that he's been "protecting" the house from her. Edric now looks to Wren to explain the ledger.
Small walled grey-stone manor on a bend of the Marrow, a day's walk downriver of Marrowford. Gatehouse with a green and white pennant, thatched village huddled against the wall. Seat of House Verrel.
Royal assessor coming to Thornhallow at noon on Day 4 to inspect the Verrel lineage charter. Known as exacting and incorruptible.

Old, half-deaf chaplain of Thornhallow's green chapel who keeps the parish register. Master Hale visited him earlier that day and warned him that "a clever young charlatan" would come asking; Osric is therefore wary of Wren. Persuasion 10 failed narrowly. He keeps a Lantern-Bearer wayside lamp lit in the chapel porch.

Examined Wren's reliquary: the parchment is genuine, an old road-priest's blessing ("Let none who bear this lamp walk unlit; let the false word fall from their tongue and the true one light the road"). Osric wept, gave Wren the register. Truth of the third descent: in the register Lord Edric's grandsire Aldous Verrel married Maud Fenn, a miller's daughter of Thornhallow, in a plain chapel rite. No Aldermere blood; Corvin altered the bride's name and house. The Verrels hold Thornhallow by an older plain land-grant, not by the descent claim, which only gave them precedence and a tax exemption. Osric keeps a second copy of the register in his own hand beneath the altar stone.
Agreed to attest the true register entry in writing and in person before Dame Crowe, on condition the Verrels are not ruined by it.

Minor house of Lady Maren Thistlewood at Ashby Weir, two days upriver of Marrowford. Corvin forged her a tale of a heroic ancestor holding a river ford, to claim ferry-toll rights. Already paid; page struck through in Corvin's draft. Toll rights are being contested by neighbouring village.

Link to Wren: old Lady Agnes Thistlewood (Maren's mother, dead) was "the lady on the spur" whom Elowen Ashgrove trusted; she probably took in a baby in a green-velvet-edged blanket about 20 years ago, then Corvin appeared with a girl-child afterward. Lady Maren may know more or may have been a child herself then.

House of Sir Corwen Dray at Saltmarsh Keep, near the estuary, three days downriver of Thornhallow. Corvin forged a betrothal contract and a vow tale tying Dray's heir to a wealthy merchant family; the merchants have since begun to doubt. Page struck through in Corvin's draft.

Ledger leaf details (Day 7): betrothal tied Sir Corwen's heir, his daughter Isaude Dray, to the Vantry merchant-house of Saltmarsh (wool and salt trade). Written beside it: sum 140 marks paid, and a date, the ninth of the month, circled, "the wedding-contract to be sealed before witnesses." That is the same ninth as the Salt Gull note.

Small wayside shrine-house of the Lantern-Bearer on the Ashby road, half a day's ride north of Marrowford. A stone hut with a bunkroom, a hearth, and a brass lamp kept lit. Run by a lay-keeper named Marta Pell, a cheerful widow. Offers free bed and bread to Lantern-Bearer faithful (Wren's Shelter of the Faithful).

Keeper Marta Pell, grey-haired, plump, green apron, warm and talkative. Corvin is a regular guest and has charmed her; she holds his sealed note for Wren. She gives Wren free bed and bread as a follower of the Lantern-Bearer.

Marta Pell: Corvin once said the brass lantern over her door and Wren's reliquary came from "the same hand", an old road-priest of the Lantern-Bearer who walked the river country about twenty years ago and vanished. Lamp base bears a tiny scratched mark: a lantern with a crooked flame and the letters "E.A.", same loops as the reliquary parchment. Corvin received both from the priest's estate; Corvin never explained how.

Day 4 morning: Lantern's Rest's travellers' book has the leaves for the season about twenty years ago cut out with a blade, cleanly, long ago (Marta never noticed; she took over fourteen years ago). The former keeper, old Hob Crannock, retired to a cottage near the ford at Ashby Weir; he might remember E.A.

E.A. = Elowen Ashgrove, a road-priest of the Lantern-Bearer, who passed Lantern's Rest ~20 years ago carrying a baby in a green blanket. Wren shares her surname (Corvin gave Wren that name; Wren's origins otherwise unknown). Elowen cut the shrine book pages herself, left lamp and blessing, went upriver to Ashby Weir, vanished. Corvin came asking after her the next spring.

Small river village on the upper Marrow where the old stone weir and ford cross; seat of House Thistlewood (Lady Maren). Ferry-toll bridge disputed. Old Hob Crannock's cottage lies by the ford. A reed-thatched inn, the Heron and Net.

Old retired keeper of Lantern's Rest, lives in a crooked cottage with a green door by the ford at Ashby Weir. Wits come and go. Remembers a road-priest named Elowen Ashgrove (the E.A.) who passed through Lantern's Rest about twenty years ago carrying a baby wrapped in a green blanket. She asked him to cut the pages of the travellers' book for that season herself, then left the lamp and a curl of blessing in a brass lantern-case. She went upriver toward Ashby Weir and was never seen again. A storyteller (Corvin) came asking after her the next spring.

Told Wren (Day 4): the blanket was edged with deep green velvet, a noble house's bolt, same as the scrap Wren holds. Elowen said she was going "to the lady on the spur", old Lady Agnes Thistlewood (now dead; her daughter Lady Maren rules there). He believes Elowen left the child in Lady Agnes's keeping; some months later a storyteller (Corvin) turned up on the Marrowford road with a girl-child of about that age, claiming he found her at a roadside shrine. Hob never saw Elowen again and does not know what became of her. Hob also says Lady Maren is not a bad woman, but afraid of the village over the toll.

Mistress of the Thistlewood manor at Ashby Weir, a tired, straight-backed woman in her forties, daughter of old Lady Agnes. Afraid of her village over the ferry-toll, which rests on Corvin's forged ford tale. Received Wren at dusk on Day 4 after reading Lord Edric's letter.

Day 4 night: Read the Thistlewood ledger leaf, accepts the ford tale is forged (she half suspected). Remembers Elowen Ashgrove staying at the manor ~20 years ago with a baby (Maren then in her twenties). Her mother Lady Agnes kept the child three months. Then Corvin arrived with a "letter in Elowen's hand" (forged) asking for the child, and Lady Agnes, ill and believing it, gave the baby up and the key to a small iron coffer Elowen had left "for the girl when she is grown". Corvin took both. The coffer itself, bearing the Lantern sign and E.A., remains in the manor's strongroom, locked; its key went with Corvin. Maren lets Wren see it.

Gave Wren a guest room, pen, and privacy on Day 4 night. Offered to stand witness against the forged ford tale before the village and will not burn the Thistlewood ledger leaf until Wren says so. Hob Crannock also willing to swear to Elowen's mark.

Small iron-bound coffer in the Thistlewood strongroom, scratched with a lantern and "E.A.". Left by Elowen Ashgrove "for the girl when she is grown." Locked; the key was given to Corvin twenty years ago. Contents unknown.

Opened Day 4 night by Wren: the brass reliquary's lantern-foot is the true key (Corvin's iron key was a decoy Elowen sent with him). Inside: a letter from Elowen to "my wren", a small silver lantern pendant, and a folded, sealed commission-paper naming Wren as Elowen's heir to her road-priest's lamp-staff. Letter: Corvin Tallowmere was Elowen's own apprentice who turned to forgery and sold her blessings; she went to confront him; if she did not return, he would come for the child with false letters. She asks her daughter to "light the road, not sell it."

Day 5 midday: Wren told the Heron and Net's crowd the truth about the ford hero. Persuasion 7: the villagers erupted, some shouting at Lady Maren to drop the toll at once, others cursing Wren as a liar paid by a rival; a man threw a tankard; the men-at-arms hustled Wren out. Word spread through the village, and Garrow was in the room, in the back by the hearth. Lady Maren's standing is damaged but the toll tale is publicly broken.
Tavern or inn in Saltmarsh named in Corvin's note, with a meeting set for "the ninth" (Day 9). Corvin intends to be there; Elowen may be too.

Day 9: the innkeeper, a wary woman named Bess Harl, would not confirm any guest. She did glance at the stair and at a locked back room, then said "no storyteller here, love" too quickly. A back room upstairs is paid up through the ninth under the name "Master Lamplighter".

Day 9 ~10:30 AM: Wren's pick failed on the back-room lock (9). Bess Harl came up the stair and caught her at it. Kit, tailing the clerk (Stealth 7), was noticed by him and he quickened toward the Vantry hall.

Day 9: Bess Harl refused Wren's gold (Persuasion 9). She says the man in the room keeps her inn afloat and has paid for her silence; she will not say who is inside. She is frightened, not loyal. She did say, grimly, that "the wedding folk at the hall will be done by noon."

Thistlewood man-at-arms, a stocky freckled woman of thirty, dry, loyal, few words. Joined Wren as a companion (Human fighter) after the fight at the ford; speared Garrow and the driver. Wears a faded blue Thistlewood tabard over chain mail, carries a longsword and shield and a light crossbow.

Wide-doored counting-and-sealing hall of the Vantry merchant-house on Saltmarsh's quay, marked with scales. Betrothal contract of Isaude Dray and the Vantry heir is to be sealed there at noon on Day 9. Doorman is a stout man in Vantry grey who demands a guild token or warrant. Side door by the salt-store opens on the clerks' passage.

Day 9 ~10:40 AM: Wren (Disguise Self as a notary's junior, Deception 7) and Kit got in by the side door via the clerks' passage. A senior Vantry clerk, Master Orrel Pike, stopped them, took the ink-pot tray, and kept Wren standing at the passage mouth near the dais curtain while Kit was told to wait by the door. From there Wren can see the sealing table and the contract case carried in by the young black-gloved clerk (Corvin's man).
